message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

**Verdict: not ready for Cabinet.** The recommendation is clearly worded, but three of its supporting claims don't hold up against the document's own figures:

- **Uniform service:** the pilot shows flats participating at less than a third of the rate of houses.
- **Local treatment:** Brookfield can take only about half the projected tonnage.
- **Fully funded:** once the tonnage is corrected, the net cost exceeds the £520,000 allocation even in the most favourable case.

Each needs fixing before the paper goes to decision-makers.

## Critical issues

### 1. Participation was not "broadly similar" across housing types
Table 1 shows **66% for houses and 21% for flats**. That gap is very large, and it undermines both the text in Section 2 and the recommendation's claim that the service "can be delivered on a uniform basis." The pilot actually points the other way: flats probably need a different approach, such as communal bins, different container sizes or targeted engagement. That approach would have costs not shown in Table 2.

### 2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce
Section 3 applies **64%**, but Table 1 gives **57%** overall. Neither figure is 64%. The pilot's 20% flats share matches the district's, so 57% is directly applicable.

| Basis | Annual tonnage |
|---|---|
| As stated (64% × 1.9 kg) | ~3,290 t |
| Pilot overall (57% × 1.9 kg) | ~2,930 t |
| By housing type (houses 66% × 1.9 kg; flats 21% × 1.4 kg) | **~2,870 t** |

The housing-type calculation is the most defensible. It comes in about 13% below the paper's figure, and it cuts the disposal saving to roughly **£212,000**.

### 3. Brookfield cannot take the projected tonnage
Section 4 says Brookfield can offer **only 1,800 t/year until 2029**. Whichever projection you use, that leaves 1,070–1,490 t/year with nowhere costed to go. The paper:
- applies the £74/t saving to all tonnage, as if everything goes to Brookfield;
- mentions the 46-mile alternative but gives no gate fee, haulage cost, or effect on vehicle and crew productivity. Long round trips could mean more vehicles than six.

"Treatment is local" is true for only about 60% of the waste.

### 4. "Fully funded" is not supported
- **Best case:** corrected tonnage, all at £38/t, no extra haulage. The saving is about £212,000 and the net cost about **£521,000**, which already exceeds the £520,000 allocation.
- **Brookfield-only saving:** 1,800 t × £74 = £133,200, giving a net cost of about **£600,000** before any cost for the surplus tonnage.
- Even on the paper's own figures, the headroom is only £30,000 (6%).
- The funding is described as "provisional" and something the Government "has indicated." The paper should say what is confirmed, for how long, and what happens if the allocation is lower.

## Significant gaps in the cost table
The author describes the costs as complete, but these items are missing or unclear:
- treatment and haulage for tonnage above 1,800 t;
- the dedicated phone line and web page (Section 6);
- crew recruitment and training;
- absence and holiday cover, and a spare vehicle (six vehicles with six crews leaves no resilience);
- supervision and management;
- whether £34,000 per operative includes on-costs (NI and pension);
- one-off costs: delivering caddies to 52,000 households, and the upfront £990,000 vehicle purchase. Showing depreciation hides the capital and cash-flow requirement.
- a flats-specific service, if one is needed (see issue 1).

## Other points to address
- **Statutory deadline:** the Simpler Recycling requirement for weekly food waste collection applied from 31 March 2026 for most English councils. The paper should state whether Thornbury has a transitional arrangement covering an April 2027 start. If it doesn't, Cabinet needs to know it is already out of compliance.
- **Timetable risk:** Cabinet has to approve within weeks to place the order by December. Vehicles arrive in March, and crews are trained on them and 52,000 caddies are delivered in the same month, with no contingency if delivery slips. A risk section with fallback options is needed.
- **Satisfaction figure:** state the survey sample size and response rate. If mainly participants responded, the 81% figure overstates satisfaction.
- **Pilot durability:** six months may capture early enthusiasm. Was participation stable, rising or falling from January to June? Weekly data was collected, so show the trend.
- **Minor:** the weighted "All" yield in Table 1 is 1.86 kg, not 1.9 kg.

## Suggested fixes before submission
1. Correct Section 2's text on flats, and either cost a flats approach or explain why one isn't needed.
2. Re-run the projection using the housing-type rates.
3. Model treatment explicitly: 1,800 t to Brookfield, the surplus to the 46-mile plant (gate fee, haulage, vehicle impact), and the position after 2029.
4. Complete the cost table, separating capital/one-off costs from recurring costs.
5. Restate the funding position honestly, with a sensitivity table (tonnage, gate fees, allocation) and the funding gap under each scenario.
6. Add a risks section covering vehicle delivery, Brookfield capacity, funding confirmation and statutory compliance.
7. Reword the recommendation to match. For example, approve the roll-out and vehicle order subject to securing treatment capacity for the surplus tonnage and confirmation of new-burdens funding, and note the expected net cost range.

The evidence base, a real local pilot measured weekly by housing type, is a genuine strength. The problem is that the paper's conclusions currently go further than that evidence supports.
